newsitem.title: USA: Energy slips at Magellan Fund, but still near top.
newsitem.headline: Energy slips at Magellan Fund, but still near top.

text.p: Fidelity's influential Magellan Fund said Wednesday that energy holdings fell to the number two position in February behind technology, occupying 13.1 percent of its $55 billion in assets.
The fund remains heavily focused on energy stocks, howevr, and the sector's recent slip in the huge portfolio is more the result of market losses than Fidelity selling, analysts said.
In January energy and technolgy were tied for the top industry slot at 14.6 percent.
"It's really due to market action rather than a conscious decision to sell energy," said Eric Kobren, executive editor of Fidelity Insight, a newsletter that tracks Fidelity.

"There may have been a little bit of selling by Magellan, but not much," Kobren said, noting energy was hurt more by the decline since February of the broader market, which has a heavy energy weighting.

Analysts note, however, that active selling probably did take place at Fidelity's Contra Fun, where in February that $24 billion fund's energy holdings slipped sharply to 16.9 percent from 21.8 in January.

Analysts said that while Magellan's energy holdings remain above the 8.2 percent weighting of the top 25 companies in Standard & Poor's 500 Index, the Contra Fund's energy weighting is widely considered to be much too high.
In February, Schlumberger Ltd, a bellwhether oil services play, slipped one slot to number eight on Magellan's "Top Ten Holdings" list, with Exxon Corp joining that list at number nine.
Royal Dutch/Shell Group, meanwhile, slipped off that list from the number nine position just below Schlumberger in January.

"Stansky's very much of a stock picker," said Jack Bowers, editor of Fidelity Monitor, a Rockland, California-based newsletter, referring to Magellan fund manager Robert Stansky, who has been at the helm since last June.
"They had been holding Royal Dutch for a while, and perhaps he thought that there was more upside potential for Exxon," Bowers said.

Indeed, whatever reservations investors may be having with energy is likely to be short-lived, and analysts say Fidelity is not likely to cut Magellan's holdings much from their current level, given the robust earnings expected this year.
"I would still expect them to continue to be in the top 10," said Donald Dion, editor of Fidelity Independent Adviser referring to Schlumberger's and Exxon's position in Magellan.
"For every buyer there's a seller. I think energy is a really attractive sector of the economy," said Fidelity Insight's Kobren.
-- Oliver Ludwig, New York Energy Desk +1 212 859 1633
